notes.h: Rural housing in the nineteenth century (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Early nineteenth-century housing in Ireland reflected the materials available locally and the wealth of each household. In the countryside the size and roof of a home told you whether the family were labourers, farmers or landowners.
points: Labourers and small farmers lived in single-storey thatched cottages, usually of two rooms (a kitchen and a bedroom), with solid stone or mud walls, which were cheap and came from the local area.
Cottages had a half-door and a small number of small windows. The half-door opened into the kitchen and could be closed at the bottom to keep animals out and let in light and air.
Thatch was made of reeds, straw or hay, and an open hearth in the main room was used for both cooking and heating, so the kitchen was the centre of family life.
Some cottages had a loft directly under the thatch, reached by a ladder, where children slept. This used the roof space as extra sleeping room without adding to the building.
Prosperous farmers lived in two-storey, slate-roofed houses with several bedrooms and a parlour (a sitting room kept for visitors), showing their greater wealth.
Wealthy landowners lived in large estate houses, with servants' quarters generally in the basement.
Diagram: a thatched cottage in cross-section, showing the thatched roof, the loft reached by ladder, the open hearth and the half-door.
notes.tip: Do not describe the thatched cottage as the home of everyone in the nineteenth century: farmers and landowners lived in larger houses. Examiners credit specific features such as the half-door, the loft and the open hearth, so name them.

notes.h: Urban housing in the nineteenth century (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Towns developed their own styles of housing, and the gap between rich and poor was very visible in the streets. Keep these urban types separate from the rural ones, because examiners do.
points: Georgian terraces in towns (rows of joined houses, for example in Georgian Dublin such as Merrion Square) were two, three or four storeys high, with basements, high ceilings and prominent doors, and were built for the better-off.
The middle classes lived in small terraced houses in the suburbs, away from the crowded town centre.
Shopkeepers often lived above their shops, which kept them close to their business.
Workers lived in small single-storey cottages or, in the towns, in crowded tenements (large buildings divided into rooms let to many families), where space and sanitation were poor.
notes.tip: For the historical development question, give one developed point per period and contrast rural and urban where you can: Georgian terraces, basements and tenements are urban features, while thatched cottages and farmhouses are rural.

notes.h: Housing in the late nineteenth century (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Better transport in the later nineteenth century changed what houses were built from and how they looked, and it changed who lived where in towns.
points: Improved transport brought a wider variety of building materials, because heavy goods such as slate could now be moved cheaply over long distances.
Houses became more ornate, with Gothic and Tudor styles.
Two-storey, slate-roofed stone buildings became the most common rural dwelling by the end of the century.
As wealthier families moved to suburban terraced houses, many large Georgian houses in towns were divided and let to poorer families, which added to overcrowding in town centres.
notes.tip: Slate replacing thatch and the dividing of Georgian houses are specific points examiners credit, so use them rather than general statements.

notes.h: Housing in the early twentieth century (Higher Level only)
notes.b: The twentieth century brought new house types and new materials, and for the first time governments played a part in providing and improving homes.
points: Detached houses (standing alone) and semi-detached houses (joined to one neighbour) appeared, along with council housing (homes built by the local authority) and new housing estates.
Brick with plaster walls replaced stone, and tiles replaced slates; two-storey houses were built where land was expensive, because building up used less land.
Rural electrification in the mid-twentieth century changed rural homes, bringing electric light and power to the countryside.
Government housing grants funded improvements to rural houses.
The slate-roofed bungalow gradually replaced the thatched cottage in rural Ireland.
notes.tip: Put council housing in this period, not the late twentieth century. Say mid-twentieth century for rural electrification, not a precise year.

notes.h: Housing in the late twentieth century (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Later in the twentieth century, housing was built in larger numbers and to higher standards, with new materials that made homes warmer and easier to maintain.
points: Private estates were built to a common design, while individual private houses varied between classical and modern designs.
High-rise blocks were built in some cities, for example the Ballymun flats in Dublin in the 1960s.
The Building Regulations (legal minimum standards for construction) greatly improved housing standards.
New materials and methods such as double glazing, PVC and fibreglass came into use, which cut heat loss and reduced maintenance.
Indoor sanitation improved, so that homes had proper indoor toilets and bathrooms.
notes.tip: Name the features examiners credit: estates, high-rise blocks, the Building Regulations and double glazing.

notes.h: Housing in the twenty-first century (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Today's housing is shaped by the cost of land, changing households and concern for the environment, so there is a much wider mix of types than in earlier centuries.
points: Twenty-first-century estates usually consist of one style but include single-storey detached, dormer and two-storey semi-detached houses, which gives a mix of homes for different households.
Apartments, townhouses and mixed-density schemes (a mix of house and apartment types on one site) are built, including gated complexes.
Old dilapidated buildings and thatched cottages are restored, and custom-designed houses are built on private sites.
Attic space is converted into rooms with Velux roof windows, and extensions, conservatories and sunroom extensions are added to many houses to give extra living space.
Modern homes include home-office space and open-plan living (a kitchen, dining and living area in one space).
Attention is paid to insulation, glazing, security, accessibility and renewable energy, reflecting greater environmental awareness.
notes.tip: Examiners credit specific features such as apartments, restored period houses and double glazing. Link the end of your answer to the earlier periods to show how styles developed.

notes.h: Why housing styles changed (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Each change in style across the centuries had causes, and naming them turns a list of periods into a developed answer.
points: Materials and transport: better transport brought slate, brick and tiles to places that once used only local materials.
Rising incomes let more families afford larger and better-built homes.
Population moved from the country to towns, which led to terraces, tenements, suburbs and later apartments.
Government housing policy and grants, and building regulations, led to council housing, rural improvements and higher standards.
Family size and land values: smaller families and expensive land led to semi-detached houses, townhouses and apartments.
Environmental awareness led to a focus on insulation, glazing and renewable energy.
notes.tip: The best answers tie each period to a cause. One line of linking text per period is enough.

notes.h: Popular housing styles in Ireland today
notes.b: Different styles suit different households, so each is popular for a reason. Tying each style to the type of household it suits is what examiners reward.
points: Bungalows are single-storey, so they suit older people, people with mobility needs and rural sites, but they need a large site. The dormer bungalow adds bedrooms in the roof space.
Two-storey detached houses suit large families and sites with space for a garden, and give privacy, but they cost more to buy and to heat.

Semi-detached and terraced houses make efficient use of land and cost less; a terraced house loses less heat than a detached house because it shares walls with its neighbours. The drawbacks are less privacy, noise from neighbours and a small garden.

Apartments and duplexes save space and maintenance and are usually in secure complexes with communal space, so they suit first-time buyers, singles, downsizers and city living. The drawbacks are limited space, no private garden and management fees.
Townhouses are multi-storey homes built on small urban sites, with limited outdoor space.
Traditional, neo-Georgian and restored period houses offer proportion and character, while modern minimalist homes are bright and easy to care for.
Custom-designed one-off houses, timber-frame and energy-efficient or passive houses are other styles, and old cottages are kept for holiday and local use in tourist areas.
notes.tip: If asked for three styles with reasons for their popularity, pick a bungalow, a two-storey house and an apartment or townhouse, and give a reason for each. For photographs, name the style, give two features and state who it suits.

notes.h: Social factors influencing the choice of housing style
notes.b: A home has to work for the people living in it, so the make-up and needs of the household strongly affect the style chosen.
points: Family size and stage, and the ages of children, decide how many bedrooms and how much space are needed, so a growing family may choose a two-storey house.
Special needs or disability may call for a single-storey home, such as a bungalow, with no stairs.
Some households want a garden or a home office, which rules out styles with no private outdoor space.
Wanting to be near family and community, and the sense of belonging this gives, can affect where and what a household chooses.
notes.tip: The best answers tie each factor to an effect on the choice, for example family size leading to a larger house. Ordinary Level questions give photographs of three styles and ask for four factors.

notes.h: Cultural factors influencing the choice of housing style
notes.b: Culture shapes what people like and what a place looks like, so it affects both what is built and what people choose to buy.
points: Personal taste, aesthetics and fashion influence choice, for example a preference for a traditional or a modern minimalist look.
Regional building traditions and local materials, such as stone or slate, shape the look of rural houses in each area.
Respect for heritage and the character of the area leads many people to restore older houses or build in keeping with their surroundings.
notes.tip: Examiners ask for social, cultural and environmental factors under headings with two points each, so keep these separate from the others.

notes.h: Economic factors influencing the choice of housing style
notes.b: Money is often the deciding factor, because it limits what a household can buy or build and what it can afford to run.
points: Income and the money available decide what a household can afford, so a first-time buyer may choose an apartment or a terraced house.
The price of land affects the cost of any style, which is why cheaper land allows larger, detached houses.
The cost of building and the running costs, such as heating, matter because a large detached house costs more to heat than a terraced one.
Resale value and investment potential matter because a home is usually a household's largest purchase.
A household also decides whether to build, buy new or buy second-hand.
notes.tip: Higher Level questions on economic factors ask for two developed points each: name the factor, then say how it affects the choice, for example cost, income, land price and resale value.

notes.h: Environmental factors influencing the choice of housing style
notes.b: The site and its surroundings affect how comfortable a home is and what may be built on it.
points: Aspect (the direction a house faces) matters because south-facing rooms gain daylight and solar heat.
Shelter from wind and rain, and exposure to them, affect comfort and heating costs.
The slope of the site affects what style can be built on it.
Energy efficiency through insulation and glazing lowers heating costs and heat loss.
The style must fit the surrounding landscape and neighbouring buildings, and planning rules control scale and materials in many areas.
Setting: a school visit to houses from different periods, or photographs of house styles, can be used to discuss their suitability to their surroundings.
notes.tip: Higher Level questions ask for the environmental factors with two developed points each: aspect, shelter, energy efficiency, fit with the landscape and planning.

keyTerms.definition: A roof covering of reeds, straw or hay, used on rural cottages in nineteenth-century Ireland.
A door divided horizontally so that the top half can be opened separately, common on rural cottages.
A row of town houses of two to four storeys, with basements and high ceilings, built in Irish towns in the eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries.
A large house or building divided into rooms or flats, each let to a separate family, common in Irish towns in the nineteenth century.
The extension of mains electricity to rural homes, which in Ireland was carried out mainly in the 1950s.
A single-storey house with rooms built into the roof space behind dormer windows.
The direction a house or room faces, which determines how much daylight and solar heat it receives.
A modern style that uses the proportions and symmetry of Georgian houses in new construction.
The repair of an older building to its original character, often supported by grants for listed or traditional buildings.

factCards.term: Three features of a nineteenth-century rural cottage
factCards.definition: Single-storey construction; a thatched roof; an open hearth used for cooking and heating.

factCards.term: Four categories of factors influencing housing style
factCards.definition: Social, cultural, economic and environmental factors.

factCards.term: Two causes of change in rural housing in the mid-twentieth century
factCards.definition: Rural electrification and government housing grants.

factCards.term: Late nineteenth-century use of Georgian town houses
factCards.definition: They were divided and let to poorer families as wealthier residents moved to suburban terraced houses.

factCards.term: Three benefits of a bungalow for older people
factCards.definition: No stairs to climb; step-free access that is easier to adapt; a compact layout that is simpler to heat and maintain.

factCards.term: Two features of a Georgian town house
factCards.definition: Two to four storeys with basements; high ceilings and prominent doorways.

questions.prompt: Describe the main features of a typical rural house in Ireland in the early nineteenth century.
questions.model: Single-storey thatched cottage with stone or mud walls and few windows; a half-door; an open hearth used for cooking and heating; a loft under the thatch reached by a ladder, where children slept. Wealthier farmers had two-storey slated houses; landowners had estate houses.

questions.prompt: Explain how social and economic factors influence a household's choice between a bungalow, a semi-detached house and an apartment.
questions.model: Social factors: family size and the number of bedrooms needed; children's ages and the need for a garden; older people or people with a disability may need a single-storey bungalow or step-free access; a single person or couple may prefer an apartment near work, amenities and transport; privacy and the wish to live close to neighbours. Economic factors: income and the money available for a deposit or building; the cost of land, which pushes urban development towards apartments and two-storey houses; running costs, with terraced and semi-detached houses cheaper to heat than detached ones; resale value and investment potential of the chosen style. Each factor should be linked to the specific style: the bungalow suits older people on a larger rural site, the semi-detached house suits a growing family in a suburb, and the apartment suits first-time buyers and downsizers in a city.
